list.listitem: Attempt to isolate and treat the underlying cause of acute lymphadenitis. Local or systemic infections frequently result in enlarged lymph nodes. C
Obtain a fine needle aspiration if fluctuance or abscess is suspected, or excisional biopsy if tuberculous lymphadenitis is suspected. C
MRSA is an increasingly common cause of abscessed lymphadenitis that fails to respond to empiric antibiotic therapy. C
Chronic lymphadenitis (longer than 4 weeks) requires workup for malignancy or mycobacterial infection. C
If multiple nodes are involved without suppuration, consider a reactive process such as a viral infection or systemic disease as the primary cause of lymphadenitis. C

background.definition: Lymphadenitis and lymphangitis are transient inflammatory reticuloendothelial responses to either focal or systemic infection. Lymphangitic carcinomatosis or tumor spread through the lymphatics of the lung, most commonly seen secondary to adenocarcinoma, will not be addressed in this chapter.

list.listitem: Enlargement of lymph nodes is the primary diagnosis in 1 in 250 visits to primary care physicians.
See Differential Diagnosis section.

In a case series of 277 immunocompetent children who underwent an incision and drainage procedure of cervical lymphadenitis, the most common bacterial causes were Staphylococcus aureus (35.7%) and Streptococcus pyogenes (18.8%). About one third of all intraoperative cultures were negative.

In another case series of children with abscessed cervical lymphadenitis, the most common organisms were also Staphylococcus aureus (63%) and group A beta-hemolytic Strep (22%). About one-fourth of Staph isolates were methicillin resistant. In another case series of 76 hospitalized children with suppurative cervical lymphadenitis, almost all (93%) of culture-positive infections in infants were caused by Staphylococcus aureus compared to 59% in children between 13 months and 5 years of age. Of the Staph isolates, 51% of were methicillin resistant.

Tuberculosis (TB)-associated lymphadenopathy is the most common extrapulmonary manifestation of TB. In a case series from Denmark, 13.5% (n = 489) of all TB patients had lymphadenopathy (annual proportions ranged from 9.4% to 15.7%); most patients were immigrants between 25-44 years of age.
Lymphadenitis has also been reported in association with herpetic whitlow (forearm node), candida albicans (cervical node), Yersinia pseudotuberculosis (inguinal node).

Kikuchi disease,also called Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease or Kikuchi histiocytic necrotizing lymphadenitis, is a rare self-limiting disorder associated with lymphadenopathy, mild fever, fatigue, and leukopenia that is associated with Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE). It is endemic in Asia but a few cases have been reported in the US; 91 cases were identified across 13 medical centers over 12 years in France. In a 7-year case series of 98 children in Singapore, 12 patients had a recurrence and one child developed SLE 10 years after diagnosis.

The lymphatic system is the principal route of transport for antigen and immune cells from tissues and serves as the initial line of defense against infections, either acute or chronic (longer than 4 weeks). Additional functions of the lymphatic system are preservation of fluid balance and fat absorption by the intestinal lymphatics.
Infections induce an antigenic response, inducing B- and T-lymphocyte activity.
Lymph nodes filter the lymph, process antigens and produce an appropriate immune response.
Reactive hyperplasia can also occur within lymphatic tissue due to a local inflammatory process such as viral or bacterial pharyngitis.
Determine whether enlargement is acute (<4 weeks) or chronic (>4 weeks) to guide further workup (). C
Determine exposure to tuberculosis, Lyme disease, cat scratch, pharyngitis, or other possible causes. C
Obtain a fine needle aspiration or excisional biopsy only for a pathologic specimen or to identify bacterial organisms to direct therapy. C
Excise the node if malignancy or Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection is suspected. C
If multiple nodes are involved without suppuration, consider a reactive process such as a virus or systemic disease as the primary cause for lymphadenitis. C

Differential.Differential_Name: Bacterial: methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA), group A Strep and group B Strep in neonates

Differential.Differential_Features: Cat or cat scratch exposure; Bartonella IgG, IgM titers beneficial; may have ocular findings including Parinaud's oculoglandular syndrome, neuroretinitis, multifocal retinitis, uveitis and retinal artery occlusion
Chronic focal node plus minus mildly positive PPD
Suspected TB contact and positive PPD; lymphadenitis can also be seen following BCG vaccination
Painless, fixed node, other systemic findings
Fever for more than 5 days and 4 of 5 major criteria including cervical lymph node larger than 1.5 cm
Other systemic symptoms: hepatosplenomegaly, renal involvement, joint involvement
Rare; most commonly seen in Asian children or women of childbearing age presenting with fever and cervical lymphadenopathy; can occur in association with SLE
Uncommon, seen in patients with immunosuppression because of HIV infection, malignancy (most often, hematolymphoid neoplasia), or iatrogenic immunosuppression

Differential.Differential_Name: Periodic fever, aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis, and cervical adenitis syndrome (PFAPA)
Differential.Differential_Features: Three to seven days of fever (39°C or more); regular cycles of 6 or more episodes; presence of pharyngitis and/or both aphthous stomatitis and cervical adenopathy; steroid responsive; normal growth and development, no known autoimmune, immunodeficiency, infectious, or malignant disorder
Association with uveitis and erythema nodosum
Associated with posterior cervical lymphadenitis; patients may report fatigue, headache and difficulty concentrating

Differential.Differential_Name: Silicone implant failure with reactive cervical nodes
Differential.Differential_Features: History of silicone gel breast implants

list.listitem: History: determine duration of lymphadenitis. Determine whether systemic symptoms, including fever, weight loss, anorexia, and arthralgias, are present to see whether an underlying malignancy or autoimmune disorder, leading to lymphadenitis, may be present. Assess for tuberculosis exposure.

Physical examination: palpate the region to determine whether a single node or multiple nodes are involved. Palpate all regions of the body to assess for involvement of distal nodes. Identify any hepatosplenomegaly, rashes, or infection in the posterior pharynx that can support or exclude possible etiologies of lymphadenitis.

Periodic fever, aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis, and cervical adenitis syndrome (PFAPA) is a rare syndrome characterized by the preceding symptoms. In a case series of 125 children with PFAPA, age at onset was 23 months and median episode duration was 3.5 days at 4-week intervals.

In another case series of 301 patients diagnosed with PFAPA from 15 centers in Europe, 90% had pharyngitis, 78% had cervical adenitis, 57% had oral aphthosis and 44% had all three clinical features. Most patients (76%) reported additional symptoms including gastrointestinal symptoms (44%), arthralgias and/or myalgias (29%), skin rashes (12%), and neurologic symptoms (3%). Just over one quarter reported a positive family history for recurrent fever or recurrent tonsillitis.
Among 83 patients with TB-associated lymphadenopathy in Denmark, most were migrants (85.5%), young with a median age of 32 years, and only 54.2% had systemic TB symptoms.

No additional diagnostic tests are required for initial diagnosis unless an abscess or malignancy is suspected. Fine needle aspiration is useful for obtaining cultures of bacterial organisms or acquiring pathologic specimens for interpretation. CBC and sedimentation rate may be abnormal but are nonspecific.

In a study of hospitalized children, those with node-first presentation of Kawasaki disease differed from those with bacterial cervical lymphadenitis in having smaller lymph nodes, lower white blood counts and higher absolute band counts and C-reactive protein levels.
Throat culture is recommended if group A Strep pharyngitis is suspected as a possible cause of lymphadenitis.

Nucleic acid amplification tests are of limited accuracy for diagnosis of tuberculous lymphadenitis. A reverse blot hybridization assay, REBA Myco-ID®, was highly sensitive and specific for detecting M. tuberculosis and non-tuberculous mycobacterium in one study. In a single institution study in Finland, in-house modifications made to the commercial T-SPOT.TB blood test using an additional purified protein derivative (PPD) antigen stimulation allowed differentiation between M. tuberculosis and non-tuberculous mycobacterium; when PPD was positive and M. tuberculosis-specific antigen was negative, the patient was diagnosed as having non-tuberculous mycobacterium unless previously vaccinated with BCG.
In another study, a multiplex polymerase chain reaction using MPB64 and IS6110 was reasonably sensitive and specific for tuberculous lymphadenopathy.

Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) tests for Bartonella henselae (the cause of cat scratch disease) lack sensitivity; this is improved by considering either positive IgG or positive IgM as a positive test. A new ELISA test employing sarcosine-soluble fraction of proteins demonstrated improved accuracy. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is more accurate.

CT scan
: It is useful in identifying deep and difficult to reach structures that may be affected by suppurative lymphadenitis. CT scan can also help to identify patients at risk for poor response to treatment of mycobacterial lymphadenitis (large necrosis, localized and extensive infiltration, and peripheral enhancement).

Magnetic resonance imaging
: It may be useful for differentiating between suppurative lymphadenitis and malignancy in necrotic cervical lymph nodes using diffusion-weighted images.

In cases of axillary metastatic lymphadenopathy when no primary tumor is identified in the breast on physical examination, mammography or ultrasound, breast MRI was found (in a systematic review of 8 retrospective studies) to detect an otherwise occult breast cancer in more than two thirds of patients with a high sensitivity but lower specificity. Histologic confirmation is suggested.

Ultrasound
: It serves as accurate method of identifying superficial suspicious cervical nodes that will require ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration.

In a case series of children with a deep lateral neck infection, there were no differences length of hospital stay or cost when using either CT scan (88 children) or ultrasound (40 children) as the primary imaging modality. Drainage was performed in 48% of each group. Thirteen children, however, had a coexisting retropharyngeal infection that was only identified on CT.

Use of superb microvascular imaging and shear wave elastography can help distinguish between benign, malignant, and normal lymph nodes with a diagnostic accuracy of 95% using vascularity index Cut-off values higher than 15%, and 99% when using a cut-off elasticity value higher than 17 kPa.
Excisional biopsy is recommended if malignancy or mycobacterial infection is suspected. Diagnosis of Kikuchi disease is also established by node biopsy.
Fine needle aspiration can be useful for suspected tuberculous superficial lymphadenitis, especially in patients with HIV.
See for a suggested approach to evaluation and treatment.
Imaging studies are usually not necessary unless an abscess is suspected.
For lymphadenitis associated with streptococcal throat infection, treat with antibiotics. C
Treat an acute, tender, erythematous node with systemic symptoms as a skin infection. C

Corticosteroids appear effective and similar to adenotonsillectomy in children with PFAPA. B The Childhood Arthritis and Rheumatology Research Alliance (CARRA) PFAPA working group identified 4 potential treatment arms: antipyretics alone, corticosteroids, colchicine or cimetidine prophylaxis, or tonsillectomy with or without adenoidectomy. C
For cat scratch disease, antibiotic treatment is not necessary for otherwise healthy patients, but a 5-day course of azithromycin can be considered. C
Excision of the node can be therapeutic in atypical mycobacterial infections. C
Incision and drainage are only recommended if acute lymphadenitis is suspected and an abscess is identified by imaging or is suspected based on clinical examination findings. C
If lymphadenitis is associated with streptococcal throat infection, treat with appropriate antibiotics.

If there is an acute, tender, erythematous node with systemic symptoms, treat with appropriate antibiotics. See chapter on skin abscess. Obtain cultures if there is an area of fluctuance using needle aspiration and treat organism as appropriate.

In the case series of children with abscessed cervical lymphadenitis noted above, methicillin-resistant Staph isolates were sensitive to clindamycin, sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim, and to a lesser extent ciprofloxacin.

For Bartonella henselae (cat scratch disease), consider a 5-day course of azithromycin. In a meta-analysis of treatment of PFAPA in children, use of antibiotics and cimetidine were ineffective. This was shown in 1 RCT to reduce lymph node volume more rapidly in the short term than placebo, although there was no difference in overall outcomes at 30 days. Other antibiotics that may be effective include rifampin, ciprofloxacin, gentamicin, trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, and clarithromycin, although clinical trials are lacking. The disease is self-limited, and antibiotic treatment is not necessary for otherwise healthy patients.

In a meta-analysis of treatment of PFAPA in children, use of antibiotics and cimetidine were ineffective. Corticosteroids appeared effective for symptom resolution, similar to tonsillectomy with or without adenoidectomy (see below). In one small randomized study of 41 children with PFAPA, low-dose steroids at 0.5 mg/kg/day were as effective as higher-dose steroids at 2 mg/kg/day in fever reduction and interval between attacks.

The CARRA PFAPA working group recommends single dose prednisone 1 mg/kg within 24 hours of fever onset and a second on day 2 of fever if there is an incomplete response for those with a fever interval <14 days. If there is an incomplete response, use a 2 mg/kg dose with future episodes. Continue the same regimen if the fever interval has improved (to >21 days for the higher dose prednisone).

For prophylaxis, this group recommends colchicine 0.5-1.2 mg daily or cimetidine 10-20 mg/kg/dose twice daily. Colchicine was effective in an open-label RCT with 18 children with PFAPA; the intervention group (colchicine 0.5 mg/day if <5 years of age, 1 mg/day if 5–10 years, and 1.5 mg/day if >10 years) had significantly fewer febrile attacks compared to the initial 3-month observation period (4.9 ± 2.3 to 1.6 ± 1.2) compared to no difference among controls (3.2 ± 1.5 to 2.7 ± 1.5).

See chapter on tuberculosis treatment if diagnosed. An RCT found that daily, self-administered rifampicin and isoniazid for 6 months was as effective as twice-weekly directly observed rifampicin and isoniazid for 6 months (including pyrazinamide for the first 2 months) for the treatment of lymph node tuberculosis.

Incision and drainage may be necessary if patients do not respond to antibiotic therapy within 48 hours and any time there is fluctuance. Nerve damage can occur when performing incision and drainage or excision.
Excision of the node can help differentiate atypical Mycobacterium infection from tuberculosis. Excision is curative for atypical Mycobacterium infection and is more effective than antibiotics alone.

In a small RCT of 50 children with nontuberculous mycobacterial cervicofacial lymphadenitis, surgical excision was more effective than curettage with respect to wound healing (3.6 ± 1.2 weeks versus 11.4 ± 5.1 weeks). Transient facial nerve weakness was observed in 4 children in the surgical group that resolved by 12 weeks.

Similarly, among 19 patients in one institution in Finland undergoing initial surgical treatment for nontuberculous mycobacterial cervicofacial lymphadenitis, those undergoing incision and curettage more often had drainage which continued for 2 or more months (3 of 13 patients), while only 2 of 6 undergoing excision of the node. experienced drainage of less than 2 weeks duration. Two patients required more than one operation, two patients had postoperative infection and one developed a hematoma.
For children with PFAPA, authors of a Cochrane review of 2 trials with 67 children found that adenotonsillectomy was effective, and tonsillectomy was probably effective.
Treat pain and fever with acetaminophen and NSAIDs if not contraindicated.
Warm compresses can decrease pain while waiting for antibiotic treatment to work.

In cases of nontuberculous mycobacterial cervicofacial lymphadenitis, observation alone may be an alternative to surgery. In a retrospective review of 52 patients in Finland, observation alone was the initial treatment in 33 (63%) and, of these, 9 resolved with no drainage and of the remainder, most had intermittent drainage through a fistula which resolved within 2 months in 13 (39%) and by all but 1 patient by one year. One patient required surgical treatment for scarring and another had recurrent swelling.
Consider referral and hospitalization if a patient is not responsive to oral antibiotics and when malignancy, autoimmune disorders, or HIV are suspected.
Also consider referral when PPD is positive, and when excision of a node is needed to direct therapy.
Prognosis is good if disease is bacterial in etiology and treated with appropriate antibiotics or if incision and drainage are performed. C
If chronic lymphadenitis or concern for malignancy exists, prognosis will depend on pathology findings. C
